characters: Odenkey: an eight-year-old Ghanaian schoolboy with short hair, wearing a yellow-and-brown check school uniform shirt and brown shorts.
Zakaria: his friendly eight-year-old Ghanaian classmate in a matching yellow-and-brown school uniform.
Nurse Azumah: a gentle Ghanaian school nurse wearing a crisp white clinical coat over a green dress, with hair neatly tied back.
Madam Kumi: the kind Ghanaian class teacher wearing a bright emerald-and-gold African-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: A worried boy’s voice for Odenkey; a kind, reassuring voice for Nurse Azumah; a warm teacher voice for Madam Kumi
narrationPlan.pace: Gentle and clear, with a reassuring ending (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

culturalNotes: The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on common diseases, including ringworm and skin diseases, and their prevention (B2.5.2.1, B3.5.2.1). Ringworm is a fungal skin infection. It spreads by touching and by sharing items such as combs and towels. It is treated by a health worker.
The story takes care that the child is not blamed. It does not say that dirt alone causes ringworm.
The story encourages children to tell a trusted adult and to get help from a nurse or health worker, and not to treat the skin on their own.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have a nurse or health worker read the story to check the ringworm facts (fungus, spreads by touch and shared items, treated with medicine from a health worker).
Check that the story is kind and avoids stigma.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about ringworm that stays calm and kind. It teaches what causes it, how it spreads, how to prevent it, and why we get help and do not tease. Based on NaCCA Science standards on common diseases and their prevention.
learningGoals: Name two ways to prevent it.
Say why we do not tease.
beforeReading: Ask: what should we do when we have a rash or an itchy patch?
whileReading: Pause on page 3 and ask: how can we stop it from spreading?
afterReading: Make a poster: do not share combs, towels and caps.
Role-play telling a teacher or nurse about a patch.
discussion: How did Madam Kumi help the class?
reflection: Who can you tell when something is wrong with your body?

support: Use pictures of items we do not share.
stretch: Write a short note encouraging a sick friend.
